activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
story:
Victoria held her slice of cake and watched Dex back away from the picnic table, his ears going pink while Cole and two other boys laughed at his rumpled jacket. "Nice outfit, Dex. Did you dress in the dark?" It was Mara's birthday party, and nobody wanted a scene, least of all Mara, who was already hurrying over with her hands out like a tiny diplomat negotiating peace.

"Guys, come on," Mara said. "It's my party."

"Chill, we're just joking," Cole said. Victoria knew that tone. Joking meant the teasing would restart the second Mara turned around. She'd seen it happen at the science club meeting last week, when Dex tried to suggest a project idea and Cole talked over him until Dex just shut his mouth and stared at the table.

Victoria stepped between the boys and the dessert table. "We're doing a game," she announced. "Round-robin style." Cole groaned. "A round-robin means each person speaks in turn around the circle," she said. "You don't get to skip, and you don't get to talk over anybody." She pointed at the picnic bench. "Sit. Best birthday memory wins the last cupcake."

Cole shrugged and sat, because it was a game and games had rules, and even he followed rules when cake was involved. They went around. Cole told a loud story about a water park. One boy described a snowstorm blackout. Victoria shared the time her grandmother set her own birthday cake on fire with too many candles, and the smoke smell had saturated the whole kitchen for days.

Then it was Dex's turn. He was quiet for a second, and nobody could interrupt, because that was the rule. "My best birthday," he said, "was when it rained and the power went out, and my dad let us build the whole birthday cake out of marshmallows and cereal because the oven was dead." Everyone laughed, the good kind, and Cole said, "Okay, that's actually exceptional," and pushed the last cupcake across the table to him.

Victoria watched Dex break the cupcake in half and hand part of it to Cole, who took it without a word. She turned to grab her drink and found Mara standing beside her, arms crossed, grinning. "Nice game," Mara said. "Too bad you planned it." Victoria frowned. "What?" Mara pointed at the table, where Cole was now asking Dex, quietly, where he'd found the cereal marshmallows. "You invented a game so nobody could tease him," Mara said. "That's the sneakiest nice thing anyone's done all day."

Victoria picked up her cup. "I have no idea what you're talking about." "Then explain why you're smiling," Mara said, and Victoria hid it behind her cup, badly.

The restaurant's big screen showed the stadium packed to the last row, and Theodore was halfway through his second basket of fries when the crowd did the wave. Thousands of people leapt up section by section, a ripple of color rolling around the bowl of seats, and the whole restaurant cheered along like the wave might somehow spill off the screen and soak them.

"That's called the Mexican wave," said Priya, his cousin, who had flown in from Manchester the night before and was now stealing his fries with impressive skill.

"The what?" Theodore said. "It's just the wave. Everybody calls it the wave." He looked around the table for backup, but his little sister was busy building a tower of ketchup packets and his dad was arguing with a menu.

"Mexican wave," Priya said again, munching. "That's what we call it at home."

Theodore could not believe two countries could have two names for the same ripple of strangers standing up. He decided to test it, because that was what you did when something sounded wrong. He climbed onto his chair, cupped his hands around his mouth, and shouted "Wave!" at the restaurant. A few people near the screen glanced over. One man in a soccer scarf lifted his arms, then sat back down, looking embarrassed.

Theodore sat, thought, and tried again. This time he yelled "Mexican wave!" The man in the scarf jumped up so fast his drink wobbled. "You know it!" he called back. He stood, raised both arms, and pointed to the left side of the restaurant, where a family of six rose in a soggy, wobbling chain, then the booth behind them, then the birthday party in the corner, all the way around the room until the wave crashed back into the man in the scarf, who sat down flushed and delighted.

"Okay," Theodore admitted, dropping back into his chair. "You win. Different countries, different words." He was already planning something bigger, though. The World Cup final was next month, and Priya would still be visiting. "We should do this at the school assembly," he said. "Half the gym yelling one thing, half the other, and we watch which one gets everyone up."

Priya grinned and pushed the empty fry basket toward him. "You'd better order more ammunition," she said. "You're going to need it."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
story:
Eli slid his thumb across the new phone's screen for the tenth time, and for the tenth time the glass answered him with a small, satisfying glow. The phone had cost him two years of birthday money and a summer of mowing lawns, and his mother had made him sit at the kitchen table and sign a paper about screen time before she would hand it over. "You budget your minutes," she had said. "The phone doesn't get to do it for you." He had signed it while the smell of her burnt toast still hung in the air.

By afternoon he had downloaded his favorite game, and by dinnertime a text arrived. YOUR ACCOUNT WILL BE DELETED IN 24 HOURS UNLESS YOU VERIFY YOUR PASSWORD. The message claimed to be from the game's official support team. Eli's stomach tightened. He had spent four hundred hours building that account. He tapped the link, and a login page appeared, gray and plain, asking for his password. He typed the first letter, then stopped. The real game company already had his password. Why would they need him to send it to them?

He tested his idea. He opened the game itself, from the icon, not the link. It loaded fine. No warning banner, no deletion notice, nothing in his inbox. Then he checked the sender of the text. The number had a strange stretch of digits, and the web address in the link, when he looked closely, had an extra letter jammed into the company's name, like a bad photocopy. The salt shaker sat cold under his fingertips as he read it twice.

"Mom," he called. She came in wiping her hands on a dish towel. He showed her the message. "It says verify or be deleted."

"That's phishing," she said. "Somebody pretending to be a company you trust, trying to get your password."

He deleted the text, blocked the number, and reported the message from inside the game's own help menu, which had a button for exactly this. His heart was still beating fast, but the beat had shifted into something steadier. He had almost handed over the keys to four hundred hours of work because a gray page looked official in the right context. He set the phone face-down on the table.

"So how was your first day with it?" his mother asked, sliding a plate toward him.

Eli picked up his fork. "Somebody tried to rob me before dinner."

She laughed. He didn't. He turned the phone back over and moved the phishing report into a folder he named, out loud, "Evidence."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
story:
Emily had been sitting at the kitchen table for twenty minutes, trying to write her social studies essay with her left hand, because her right arm was wrapped in a bright green cast from wrist to elbow. The essay was about tariffs, and she had managed one sentence: "A tariff is a tax on goods that come from another country." Her pencil grip was clumsy, and the words on the page looked like they had been written during an earthquake.

Then the itch started. It began as a small tickle under the cast, right near her wrist, and grew into a fire. Emily squirmed. She shook her arm. She pressed her palm against the cast and pushed, which did nothing at all. Her eyes drifted to the plastic ruler lying beside her essay, thin and flat and perfect.

She was sliding the ruler toward the edge of the cast when her little brother Theo walked in, eating a granola bar. "Mom said dinner's in ten minutes," he said. Then he saw the ruler. "Are you going to scratch with that? Mom told me the doctor said not to. She said doctors warn against sliding objects like pencils or sticks into a cast, because they can scrape the skin and damage the cast's lining."

Emily froze with the ruler halfway to her wrist. "Great. Now what do I do?"

"You could bang on it," Theo offered, and he rapped his knuckles on the hard green surface. The vibration traveled down, and for one second the itch faded. Emily grabbed a wooden spoon from the counter and tapped the cast gently, once, twice, like a woodpecker. It worked, a little, but the itch always crept back.

"We need a real plan," she said. She thought about the cool pack of frozen peas in the freezer. Cold might travel through the cast where scratching couldn't. Theo fetched the peas and held them against the itchy spot while Emily kept tapping. Between the cold and the tapping, the fire dulled to a small ember.

"That's the most eloquent solution to an itch I've ever seen," Theo said, mouth full of granola.

"It's not eloquent, it's desperate," Emily said, but she was smiling. "You should advocate for the peas method at school. You could make posters."

"Poster number one: The Ruler Is Not Your Friend."

Emily laughed so hard the peas slipped, and Theo lunged to catch them before they hit the floor.

The living room was so crowded that Christopher ended up on the floor with his back against the couch, wedged between his cousin Marisol's knees and the coffee table. On the screen, the game was tied with two minutes left, and Uncle Ray kept standing up whenever his team scored, which blocked the diagonal view from the armchair where Grandpa sat. During a timeout, a commercial for sneakers came on, and Marisol said, "Wait. Why do they even call it a basket? Nobody's shooting into a basket. It's a hoop with a net."

"Because it used to be a real basket," Christopher said. "A peach basket."

"You made that up," Marisol said, and Uncle Ray laughed from the kitchen doorway, which Christopher took as a signal that the whole room was about to humiliate him if he didn't produce proof. He had read it somewhere, in Grandpa's old sports almanac, but he couldn't remember where the book was now. While everyone argued about whether the referee had missed a foul, Christopher crawled along the floor to the shelf under the window, where the almanac lived between a dictionary and a stack of TV guides. He found the entry under basketball and ran his finger down the page.

"James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891 at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts," he read, "using peach baskets as the goals. Peach baskets. That's why it's called basketball. They didn't cut holes in the bottom at first, so somebody had to climb up and get the ball out every time somebody scored."

Marisol leaned over his shoulder to see the page herself. "Huh," she said. "You weren't making it up." Uncle Ray came back in with chips and said, "That's actually true. They used peach baskets." Christopher felt himself grinning, but then the game came back on and Grandpa stood up fast, and the almanac slid off Christopher's lap onto the carpet, page down, spine bent.

Grandpa's team lost by one point on a shot at the buzzer, a long diagonal runner that banked in off the backboard. Grandpa sat down slowly and didn't say anything for a while. Marisol picked up the almanac and smoothed the bent page with her thumb, and Uncle Ray turned the TV off, which felt strange after all that noise. "Next timeout," Marisol said quietly, "tell me the one about why it's called a foul." Christopher shrugged and looked at Grandpa's face, decided against talking for a minute, and passed his grandfather the last chip from the bowl between them.

"December 1891," Grandpa said at last, shaking his head. "Peach baskets. And my team still can't make a free throw."

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
story:
Hazel sat cross-legged on Priya's bedroom floor with a laptop on her knees and a printout of survey answers beside her. The student council had asked every kid in the school which lunch activity they wanted, and Hazel, as the new data person, was supposed to summarize the results by grade before Monday. Priya's older brother had shown them spreadsheets once, but he was at soccer now, and the screen in front of Hazel looked ominous, a gray grid stretching in every direction with hundreds of rows of answers below it.

"Just count them by hand," Priya said, flopping onto her bed with a notebook. Her real ambition this semester was to design the posters for whichever activity won, and she wanted to know the winner early so she could start sketching. "There can't be more than four hundred."

"There are six hundred and twelve," Hazel said. She envied Priya's confidence. Counting by hand would take all weekend, and she would still have to sort it by grade afterward. She scrolled through the columns: A was the grade, B was the activity, C was the student's reason. Somewhere, she remembered, there was a thing called a pivot table that could do the counting for her, but she had never made one.

She tried clicking through the menus. Rows went where columns should go, and the numbers came out as a nonsense total of 612 for every cell. She stared at it. "It's counting everything at once," she said slowly. "I need it to split by grade and then count within each grade." She dragged the grade heading into the rows box and the activity heading into the values box, and suddenly the grid rearranged itself, small counts appearing under each grade like magic.

Priya leaned over her shoulder. "Wait, can it tell us the sixth grade specifically? Text my brother, he's better at this." She sent a message, and when the reply buzzed in, she read it aloud: "He says look at C4. That's the cell in column C, row 4."

Hazel frowned at the screen. She clicked on a cell and the box at the top of the screen showed its address. The one she had picked was C4, and it sat in the third column over and the fourth row down. So that was how it worked: the letter was the column, the number was the row. She moved her cursor to check, and sure enough, C5 was directly beneath C4, same column, next row.

But something was wrong. The value in C4 said 47 sixth graders wanted chess club, and that didn't match what she remembered scrolling past. She looked again at how she had dragged the fields. The grade labels had landed in the values box by mistake, so the table was counting the wrong thing. She fixed it, dragging grade to rows where it belonged, and the numbers shifted, chess club dropping to 31.

"Which one's winning?" Priya asked, pencil already hovering over her notebook.

"Art club, in every grade except eighth," Hazel said. "Eighth grade wants the podcast booth."

Priya gasped and started drawing microphones. Hazel scrolled back to the raw answers to double-check one of the counts, her finger moving down column B, row by row. "Two, three, four, five," she murmured, "all podcast."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
story:
Lucas tapped his pencil against the rainfall graph for the Thar Desert and frowned. The bar for July shot up like a skyscraper next to the flat little bumps of the winter months, and that did not make sense to him. Deserts were supposed to be dry. The classroom smelled like chalk and the wet rain jackets hanging by the door, and outside the window a steady drizzle streaked the glass.

His teacher had paired the class off to compare a desert climate with a rainforest climate using rainfall and temperature graphs, and Lucas had ended up with Priya, who sat two rows over and always finished her math early. She slid her laptop toward him. "You have to look at this," she said.

On the screen were two satellite images of the same patch of Earth, the Indian Ocean and South Asia. The January picture showed a bright band of clouds sitting in a line south of India, hugging the equator like a belt. The July picture showed the same band, except it had moved north, parked right over India and the surrounding land. Lucas leaned closer until he could smell the laptop's warm plastic fan.

"That's weird," he said. "The clouds moved."

"They're not just any clouds," Priya said. "My cousin in Chennai calls that band the Intertropical Convergence Zone."

Lucas copied the name onto his worksheet, then looked back at his two graphs. The rainforest station in Borneo got soaked every single month, no favorites, steady as a metronome. The desert station got almost nothing all year, except for that one tall tower of rain in summer. He turned his pencil around and held it over the July satellite image, lining it up with the cloud band. Then he slid the pencil north, over the land, and tapped the screen.

"So in January the band hangs down south, over the ocean, and the desert stays dry," he said slowly. "In northern summer the whole thing shifts north over South Asia, and when it does, the rain comes with it." He picked up his graph again. "That's my July tower. That's where all that rain is from."

"That would explain why my aunt says it pours every afternoon in July," Priya said. Her grin was infectious, and even Lucas's frown came undone.

He had a small worry, though. What if he had the direction wrong and the band actually drifted south in summer, the way some kids in his class insisted? That little controversy had started an argument at the back table, and the thought of it started to irritate him. He scrolled back to the January image, then forward to July, checking the coastline of India against the edge of the cloud band. In January the band's southern edge sat below the land. In July the band lay across it. North. It moved north. He wrote it down.

Priya tilted the laptop so the back table could see. "Hey, look at this," she called.

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
story:
The computer lab smelled like warm plastic and the lemon cleaner Mr. Dorsey used on the keyboards, and Abigail had exactly one class period to make her science project page work. The heading needed to be centred, which her notes said meant CSS, and the table of her beetle data needed to appear below it. She had already fixed the heading, typing "text-align: center" and watching the title slide to the middle of the screen like magic she had performed herself.

"Install it on the school site before lunch and you're safe," said Marcus, leaning over from the next computer. He had been hovering all morning, offering help she hadn't asked for, and every time she glanced at him he looked away a little too quickly.

"I haven't even got the table working," Abigail said. She had written a short Python program to print her data, fourteen weeks of observations, each row showing the length of the larva she had measured. When she ran it, only one row appeared on the page: the last one, week fourteen, sitting there alone. She ran it again. Same thing. One row.

"Maybe the loop's broken," Marcus said, but his voice was vague, as if he weren't really guessing.

Abigail stared at the program. The loop looked fine. It said "for week in weeks," and then a line that printed the week and the length. She counted the rows in her data. Fourteen. She counted the rows printed. One. Somewhere, thirteen rows were vanishing, and she couldn't see where they went.

She leaned close to the screen. The print line sat flush against the left margin, while the "for" line above it also sat flush. She had a vague memory of copying an example from the board, but the board was erased now. She tried an experiment, the kind her mother called "change one thing." She pressed the space bar four times in front of the print line, so it slid to the right, tucked under the "for" like a chick under a wing.

She ran the program. Fourteen rows spilled onto the page, week one through week fourteen, every measurement accounted for. So the spaces mattered. The indented line belonged inside the loop, running again and again, once for each week. And before, unindented, it had run only once, after the loop had finished, which was why the last row, and only the last row, had shown up. She tested it once more to be sure, pushing the line back to the margin and watching the table collapse to a single row again.

"Marcus," she said slowly, "did you already know that?"

He pushed his chair back an inch. "Maybe I ran into it yesterday. On my own page."

"You've had a finished page since yesterday and you watched me struggle for an hour?"

"I wanted to see if you'd figure it out," he said, "because I didn't. Mr. Dorsey had to tell me." He pulled up his own screen, and there it was: his heading centred, his table complete, and at the bottom, in small letters, "Thanks to A. for the beetle data."

"That's my data," Abigail said. "That's my whole project on your page."

"I asked Mr. Dorsey if we could present together," Marcus said. "He said to ask you."

Abigail saved her file, installed the page on the school site with two minutes left in the period, and looked at her centred heading shining above fourteen tidy rows. "Then ask me," she said, and turned the screen so the whole class could see it.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
story:
Sarah stood in the living room holding a spatula like a microphone and waited for her cousin Marcus to stop giggling. They were practicing improv because the community theater held auditions on Saturday, and the director had said the whole audition would be one scene with a partner. The rule, as Sarah understood it, was a principle called "yes, and": whatever your partner offered, you accepted it and added something of your own.

"Okay," Marcus said, still snorting. "You're a tour guide and I'm a tourist. Go."

"Welcome to the museum of famous speeches," Sarah began, sweeping her arm toward the couch. "You've arrived just in time."

Marcus crossed his arms. "This is dumb. Two minutes? You can't say anything important in two minutes."

Sarah almost argued, and then she remembered what had stopped her the same way last week. Their grandmother had been telling the story of a school assembly, how a boy in her class had stood up in 1963 on the anniversary of a famous speech and recited the Gettysburg Address from memory, all of it, while the principal watched the clock. "Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, given on November 19, 1863, was about 272 words long and took roughly two minutes to deliver," Grandma had said, tapping the arm of her chair. "Longest two minutes of that principal's life, and the most important thing anyone said all day."

Instead of arguing, Sarah said, "Yes, and that's exactly why this museum is special." She pointed the spatula at the bookshelf, holding it perfectly perpendicular to the floor like a real pointer. "Every famous speech here was under three minutes. Two minutes is plenty. Watch." She cleared her throat and began reciting the opening lines she'd memorized from the poster in the hallway. "Four score and seven years ago..."

Marcus blinked. He had expected her to fold, and she hadn't. "Yes, and," he said slowly, catching on, "you're the ghost of Lincoln, and you've been trapped in this museum for a hundred years."

"Sarah accelerated toward the kitchen, her coat tails, which were really just Dad's old jacket, flying behind her. "Yes, and I've been living on the snacks in the gift shop. Follow me, tourist, before the curator catches us."

Marcus chased after her, no longer giggling but actually running lines, his voice deepening into a ghostly boom. They careened around the kitchen table twice, and when Sarah finally collapsed into a chair, breathless, Marcus flopped into the one beside her and slid the cookie jar across the table without being asked, because he knew she'd want one after all that.

"Saturday," he said, "when we audition, do you think they'll give us a scene that good?"

"Better," Sarah said, and broke the cookie in half.

story:
Avery spread the two graphs across the library table and weighted the corners with pencils before the air conditioning could send them fluttering. One showed monthly rainfall in the Sonoran Desert, a flat line that barely lifted off the bottom of the page. The other showed a rainforest in Borneo, where the bars towered so high they looked like a solid wall. The clock above the reference desk read 4:12, and the library closed at five. Her project was due first period tomorrow, and she still didn't have the answer to the question her teacher had posed: why does the same crop fail in one wet place and thrive in another?

She needed a picture of a rainforest farm for her poster. Her younger brother, Marcus, sat across from her with a bandaged thumb he would not stop examining, ever since Mom had warned him that a cut could get an infection if he kept picking at it. He flipped through a book about Asian agriculture while Avery hunted for photographs.

"Wait," Marcus said. "This doesn't make sense. This farmer is planting rice seedlings in a little bed, like a garden. And then these other people are sticking rice plants into a flooded field. Are they planting it twice?"

Avery was hesitant to believe him, because Marcus got things wrong constantly, like the time he insisted fog was smoke from the ocean. But she leaned over and looked. On one page, seedlings crowded together in a small nursery bed, green and stubby as new grass. On the facing page, rows of people bent over a flooded paddy, pushing young plants into the water one by one, by hand. She turned the pages back and forth. Same crop. Two plantings.

"So they start it in a nursery bed," she said slowly, "then transplant it into the flooded field." The pieces began to click against her graphs. The rainforest's enormous rainfall, the flooded fields in the photographs, they belonged to the same story. She grabbed a marker and wrote it out: rice grown first in a nursery bed, then transplanted, often by hand, into flooded paddies. The desert graph, with its stingy slivers of rain, could never flood a field like that. The rainforest could.

"Does that help?" Marcus asked, sounding worried the answer might be no.

"It fixes everything," Avery said. The clock said 4:47. She taped the graphs onto her poster, added the photograph of the farmers bent over the water, and wrote her headline in tall letters: WHERE THE RAIN GOES. A librarian began wheeling a cart toward the shelves, locking the cabinet doors one by one, and Avery slid her poster into her backpack just as the lights over the reference desk blinked twice.

"That's a five-minute warning," the librarian called out.

Avery zipped the bag and held it against her chest. "Race you to the door," she said.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
story:
The nature trail behind the school had a wooden bench near the creek, and that was where Isla set up the field kit her science teacher lent her: a pocket microscope, a razor blade, a dropper of iodine, and an onion she had carried in her backpack all morning. Her assignment was due Monday. She had to peel a thin layer of onion skin, stain it, and draw the cells with the wall, the membrane, and the nucleus labeled. She could have done it in the lab after school on Friday, but she had chosen the trail instead, the way she had chosen a solo hike last summer instead of going with her friends. She still wasn't sure that had been the right call, but this one felt like it might be.

Her friend Marisol found her there, as she somehow always did. "You really brought an onion on a nature walk," Marisol said, sitting down on the bench without waiting for an invitation. Isla peeled a translucent strip of skin from the onion's fleshy layer, laid it on the slide, and added a single drop of iodine. Under the pocket microscope, the cells appeared like pale bricks in a wall, each one bordered and neat. She began to draw them in her notebook, labeling the thick outer wall first, then the thin membrane pressed just inside it. The nucleus showed up as a darker dot once the stain soaked in, and she marked that too.

"That's good," Marisol said, looking over her shoulder at the finished drawing. Then she flipped back a page and stopped at Isla's comparison chart from last week's homework. "Wait. You wrote mitochondria as animal-only." Isla's pencil hovered, hesitant, over the chart. She had been proud of that chart. She remembered arguing her logic at the dinner table: animals eat food, so animal cells would need something to release energy from it, and plants make their own food, so they wouldn't need any such thing. At the time the reasoning had seemed airtight.

"Plants have mitochondria too," Marisol said. "Both plant and animal cells have them. They release energy from food." Isla frowned at her drawing of the brick-shaped cells. "But plants make their own food," she said. "Yeah," Marisol said, shrugging. "They still need mitochondria anyway." Isla turned back to the microscope and looked again at the onion cells, imagining the tiny structures she could not see at this magnification, working away inside a layer of skin thinner than paper. She couldn't justify leaving the chart the way it was. She crossed out the animal-only box and rewrote the column.

"It's kind of irony," she said slowly, "that the plant makes its own food and still needs the thing that gets energy out of it." Marisol raised an eyebrow. "That's not really how you use that word." "It's close enough," Isla said, and bent over the slide again, because the light had shifted and a row of nuclei had come into view, each dark dot sitting inside its cell like a seed inside a translucent fruit. She drew them one by one, pressing hard enough that the pencil nearly went through the page.

Last spring, her grandmother had come over with a bag of postcards, and when Peyton said her class trip had been interesting, her grandmother had leaned forward and asked what exactly was interesting about it. Peyton had stammered something about the bus and then, finally, described the moment a hawk had landed on the fence outside the planetarium and stared at them through the glass while everyone was still arguing about lunch. Her grandmother had laughed and said she could see the whole thing, hawk and all. "Nice" had shown her nothing; the hawk had shown her everything.

"So the vague ones," Peyton said slowly, tapping her pencil, "words like nice, good, interesting. They give me my opinion without showing anything." Marcus nodded. "Right. A concrete detail lets me picture it and judge for myself." She crossed out "nice" and wrote, "The grandmother picked up a wet feather and rolled it between her fingers." Then she crossed out "good trip" and wrote that Jules had counted forty-one dead jellyfish on the sand and kept the number in his head like a prize.

Now she needed a climax, the moment everything turned. She had been avoiding it because it felt ambiguous, like she couldn't tell what her story was really about. "Maybe that's the problem," Marcus said. "The climax has to be the moment it turns. Yours is just people talking on a beach forever."

They formed an alliance: Marcus would read every page out loud, and Peyton would not defend anything until he finished. When he read the jellyfish line, he stopped. "The grandmother should find one that's still alive," he said. "Right there. That's your turn." Peyton wrote it: the grandmother kneels, the jellyfish pulses once against her palm, and Jules has to decide whether to leave it for the tide.

At four the next day, she handed the printed pages to the librarian at the front desk, one minute before the deadline. "First entry this year," the librarian said, stamping the corner. Peyton smiled, took back her copy, and on the way out she stopped to look through the window at the parking lot, where a crow was standing on the hood of a silver car, watching the doors like it was waiting for someone.

Tyler leaned in. The heading "GODZILLA: REPTILE OF THE BASEMENT" sat stuck in the corner of the page, and below it was a box where you typed a number and the page told you if it was prime. Tyler typed 97 and pressed the button. The page froze. The cursor spun. Godzilla stared, unblinking, a true carnivore waiting for something to move. "It does that on big numbers," Marcus admitted. "Ava's going to think my page is broken. This could demolish my whole reputation."

Tyler added text-align: centre to the heading first, because that part he actually knew, and watched the title glide to the middle. Then he turned to the prime checker. Marcus's code tested every number from 2 up to the one you typed, one at a time, asking each, "Do you divide it evenly?" On a huge number that was millions of questions. Tyler traced the code with his finger, line by line, and noticed something odd: right after the code checked whether the number was divisible by 2, it kept testing 4, then 6, then 8, all the even ones, all the way up.

He had a guess, but he wanted proof before he said anything out loud. In a new file he tried 15 with only the odd tests, 3, 5, 7, 9, and it still said not prime, correctly, because 3 caught it. He tried 21, 35, 49. All found, all by odd divisors. He could not make it fail. "Skip the evens," he said finally, deleting half the checks. "After checking whether a number is divisible by 2, you only need to test odd divisors. An odd number can never be divided evenly by an even one." Marcus squinted at the screen. "That's it? That's the whole trick?" "Run it."

Marcus typed 999,983 and pressed the button, and both boys held their breath, because if the page froze now, everything was over. The answer appeared before Godzilla could even blink. Prime. The heading beamed from the centre of the screen like a trophy. Marcus grabbed his phone to text Ava, then stopped, staring at the instant result. "It's done already? But she loved watching it think." He typed 999,983 again, slower this time, and waited for a freeze that never came.

Kate stood by the ice freezer with her bike helmet under one arm, watching her neighbor Mr. Alvarez feed the pump like it might run out any second. "They're saying the refinery in Baytown might shut down," Mr. Alvarez told her, waving his receipt. "Everybody fills up at once, and boom, the price jumps. Scarce and wanted, that's all it takes."

"Then why is the water still a dollar?" Kate asked. He shrugged toward the rack, which was crammed with bottles, rows and rows of them. Plenty of something, cheap price. Scarce something, high price. She turned that over all the way home, because it reminded her of something, and the something made her stomach hurt.

At school, everyone had been trading Stellarbeast cards since September. Kate owned the rarest one, a Moonfang Holo that Tavo had offered forty cards for in December, back when the hallway trades got so loud that Mrs. Okonkwo had to move desks to obstruct the flow of kids crowding around the card tables. Kate had almost said yes that day, but she'd been impulsive before and regretted it, so she held out. In January, Tavo offered sixty. Moonfang Holos were barely circulating anymore; nobody would trade theirs away. It was like a principle she couldn't quite name, something invisible pushing the numbers up and up.

That night she looked it up for a history project and found a strange page about the Dutch Republic, where prices for rare tulip bulbs had soared in the winter of 1636 to 1637. People trading bulbs in taverns, paying fortunes for a single flower. Then the page said the whole thing collapsed in February 1637, when buyers stopped showing up. Kate read it twice. Nobody had banned tulips. Nobody had burned the bulbs. The buyers had just stopped coming, and that was enough.

The next morning she found Tavo by the gym and made her offer before she could lose her nerve. "Forty cards, today, for the Moonfang." Tavo stared at her like she was a step behind. "Nobody's trading those anymore. Devon's selling his for ten. Dax gave his away yesterday." Behind him, Kate could see the corner where the trading crowd used to gather. Two kids sat there now, doing homework. She traded anyway, took Tavo's best twenty for it, and put the Moonfang in her backpack next to her history notes, where the doomed tulips sat on their printed page, beautiful and worthless at exactly the same moment. On the way out, she passed the vending machine, still selling water for a dollar.

story:
Penelope had been practicing her backward crossovers for two weeks, and today was the day they had to work, because Marcus was picking her up at the rink at noon for their first date. She circled the rink once, testing the ice, then caught the boards as her skate slid out from under her.

"Smooth," said Dana from the snack bar window, where she was supposed to be working but mostly watched the skaters and ate pretzels she wasn't allowed to consume on shift.

"Ten minutes," Penelope said. "I have ten minutes to fix this."

She thought about it while she skated. It wasn't the ice, because Dana had been out earlier and hadn't slipped. It wasn't her skates, because she'd had them sharpened Friday. It had to be the left edge, and it only failed on the crossover, which meant she was leaning wrong, putting her weight somewhere she couldn't see. So she tried an experiment: she crossed over slower than slow, counting, and felt it. Her hip dropped a beat before the turn. When she held the hip up, the edge held too.

Marcus arrived at 11:58 with his helmet under his arm and his little sister, Ruby, trailing behind him like a shadow with opinions.

"She has to come," he said. "Babysitter canceled. Is that weird? Tell me if it's weird."

"It's weird," said Ruby. "Also, I want to see the vampire movie at four, and you said I could pick, and now you're saying I can't, which is lying."

"Ruby wants the one with all the fangs," Marcus said. "I keep telling her no."

Penelope glided a lap while they argued. She'd heard her dad mention once that the vampire one was rated PG-13, and Ruby was only nine. Her dad had said the rating came out on July 1, 1984, right between PG and R, as a new step, because apparently PG and R were too far apart for some movies. She filed that away.

"What's it rated?" she asked.

"PG-13," Ruby said. "I checked twice."

"There's your answer. It's not PG and it's not R. It's the one in between, the step they made in 1984, on the first of July. Nine-year-olds can't just walk in."

Ruby narrowed her eyes like she suspected a trap. "Fine. The panda movie. But I get popcorn, a large, and you carry it."

Penelope demonstrated the crossover, clean and slow, then fast, and it held. Marcus applauded with his helmet, which made a hollow bonk sound, and Ruby laughed so hard she had to sit down on the skate rental counter.

"So," Marcus said, wobbling onto the ice and grabbing her elbow immediately. "Show me that backward thing? Before we both need knee surgery or whatever that bendy part is called."

"Cartilage," Penelope said. "And my grandma says bad knees are hereditary, so be careful. I come from a long line of people falling down."

She set her hip, took his hand, and started the turn.

story:
The folded note from Coach Ruiz landed on the bleacher beside Jeremy's gym bag: "You're authorized to call the plays Friday. Point guard means the game runs through you." Practice started in ten minutes, and Jeremy still could not decide how to run the pick and roll against Eastside, whose big men switched every screen.

He dribbled at the foul line, imagining it. Marcus would slide over and set the screen. Jeremy would rub shoulders with him, and either the defender switched and Jeremy passed to a rolling Marcus, or nobody switched and Jeremy drove. The problem was that Eastside always seemed one step ahead, and Jeremy could not see why. There had to be a pattern in their switches, something hidden in how they moved.

Before the scrimmage, Coach had the team run hurdles along the sideline. Jeremy clipped the third hurdle and stumbled through it, landing flat-footed. Marcus sailed over every one, but Derek, the fastest sprinter on the team, kept knocking them down or floating so high in the air that he landed slow, well past the hurdle, his lead leg swinging up stiff and straight like a plank. "You're hanging up there," Jeremy said. Derek tried again and hung there again.

Jeremy watched him closely. Marcus bent his lead knee and drove it over the hurdle first, then straightened the leg on the way down, and he came off each hurdle low and quick. Derek swung his whole leg up rigid, and that lifted his body too high, so he drifted over the top instead of running through it. "Lead knee first," Jeremy called. "Then straighten it." Derek nodded, drove the knee, straightened, and snapped down over the fourth hurdle without touching it. "That's it," Derek shouted, already three hurdles clear.

Jeremy chewed on that through a water break. The thing that ruined Derek's hurdling was not slowness. It was doing a stiff, obvious move that pushed him too high and left him floating where everyone could read him. At the whiteboard he texted his older cousin Rene, who had played point guard at Wilson High: "Eastside reads my drives. What do I do?" Rene's reply buzzed back fast: "If they see the play coming, you've already lost. Make the screen look like one thing, then let it become another. You have until Friday. Figure out the pattern in their switches; every team has one."

So Jeremy made his screen look stiff and obvious, a plank of a move, the same screen every time, for three possessions in the scrimmage. He watched. The switching big man always floated toward the ball, high and slow, sure of himself, reading the obvious move. On the next possession Jeremy called " forty-one," sent Marcus to the wing, and came off a screen that looked like the same plank play, except he bent it, changed direction at the last instant, and hit the approximate gap between two slow-moving defenders. Marcus rolled, Jeremy flicked the pass, and the ball dropped through without touching iron. "That," Derek yelled from the sideline, one hand raised mid-hurdle, "looked nothing like the other ones."

story:
Annabelle got to the microscope station second, right behind Marcus, which meant she had to watch him hog the good scope for five whole minutes while she waited with her onion and her lab sheet. On the sheet, three words waited for arrows: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus. She had already peeled a paper-thin layer of skin off the onion with tweezers, and it lay on her slide like a ghost of an onion, pale and wrinkled.

Her first slide was a disaster. She dropped the coverslip flat onto the skin, the way you would clap a book shut, and when she looked through the eyepiece she saw dozens of round black-edged circles clustered everywhere. She drew them quickly, three of them, and labeled one "nucleus" before a doubt crept in. They were awfully round. And awfully empty.

"Those aren't cells," said Priya from the next station, leaning over. "Those are air bubbles. You've got a whole sky of them."

Annabelle sat back. Bubbles. She had trapped a pocket of sky between glass and glass, and she had almost turned it in for a grade. She pulled the elastic band off the slide box, snapped it once around her wrist, and thought. The bubbles had to be air that got in when she dropped the coverslip straight down, trapping it under. So maybe the trick was not to drop it flat. Maybe she could let one edge touch first and lower the rest slowly, like closing a door instead of slamming it.

"Try it," Priya said, though Annabelle hadn't said anything out loud. "You look like someone about to advocate for a big idea."

"I am advocating for it," Annabelle said. "Angle. One edge first." She took a fresh piece of onion skin, laid it flat, added the drop of stain, and touched just the edge of a new coverslip to the liquid. Then she lowered it slowly, hinged on that first edge, letting it settle across the skin like a slow shield coming down.

Through the eyepiece, the circles were gone. Instead the field filled with boxes, rows and rows of brick-shaped cells stacked together, their walls outlined clean and dark. Near the center of one cell sat a denser dot, round and small. She found it in the next cell too, and the next. That had to be the nucleus, and the dark border around each box had to be the wall, with the membrane just inside it, thin as a whisper.

She drew it all, arrows and labels, while Marcus complained that his slide looked like a meteor shower. "Bubbles," she told him, turning her drawing around. "Lower it at an angle, one edge first. Want to see mine?" She slid off her stool and waved him toward her scope, and Priya crowded in behind, and above them the ceiling fan spun like a propeller, stirring the smell of onion through the whole lab.

story:
Cameron was halfway through his pasta when his phone buzzed against the table leg. His mother gave him the look, so he angled the screen under the edge of the table like a skilled artisan of not getting caught. It was a photo from Dex: his new bike leaning against a garage, captioned "guess who saved up all summer."

"Phone on the counter," his mother said. Cameron slid it over, screen up, which was a tactical error.

His little sister Priya grabbed it before it stopped moving. "Why is there a map on Dex's bike picture?"

"There isn't," Cameron said. "Photos don't have maps."

"There is a little pin thing. It's showing a street." She turned the phone toward their mom. "It says Maple Court."

Cameron reached for it, and Priya, being Priya, held it out of reach and read aloud. "Photo taken at, then a bunch of numbers. Then it says location on."

Something cold crawled up the back of his neck. He took the phone, opened the photo, and tapped the little "i" in the corner himself. Sure enough, there was the map, and there was the pin, sitting squarely on Maple Court, which was where Dex lived, which Dex had told the whole group chat never to share because his older brother said people online were naive about exactly this kind of thing. Cameron had laughed at that. Now he was looking at a map to his friend's house that Dex had transmitted to eleven people without knowing it.

"Language," his mother said mildly, because apparently he had said something out loud.

"Mom, when a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file," Cameron said. "Dex told me yesterday. It's called EXIF metadata. I thought he was making it up."

"So every photo knows where it was taken," Priya said, chewing bread.

"Ours do, apparently." Cameron was already scrolling. Two weeks ago he had posted twelve pictures of the tree fort he and Dex had built behind his grandfather's shed, and he had captioned them "secret fort, no girls, no adults, no exceptions," which at the time had seemed hilarious. Every one of those photos had a map pin on his grandfather's back acreage, down to which tree, basically. Anyone who looked at the file's details could find it. Anyone at all. Strangers. He had felt like the fort was hidden because it was behind a shed, which now struck him as roughly the level of planning that went into hiding a sandwich by putting a napkin on it.

He texted Dex: check the i on your bike photo. Then delete it. Then he went through his own posts, one by one, and removed the fort pictures while his pasta went cold and Priya narrated his facial expressions to their mother.

"Regret," she announced. "With a side of horror."

Dex's reply arrived as Cameron was carrying his plate to the sink. "DELETED. also I'm telling my brother he was right. he's going to be insufferable forever."

Cameron typed back, "worth it," deleted that too, and wrote, "meet at the fort tomorrow. new rule: location services off before the door opens."

She thought about her aunt's paperback on the picnic table at home, the one with the marriage researcher's name on the spine, John Gottman. Aurora had flipped through it mostly to be nosy, but one page had stuck. A complaint, the book said, was about one specific action. Marisol stopped dragging her toe. "That's it? No 'you never keep secrets, you're basically a walking megaphone with good hair'?"

Aurora stared at the screen. So her whole case had rested on a biased theory, built from one clue: Sam knew, and Sam and Marisol texted constantly. "I will. After the dampness." She ran, and Marisol was right behind her, yelling, "If you splash me, that's a complaint about one specific action, and I will forgive it!"

story:
Felix's grandfather had died on Tuesday night, room 414, with the TV still murmuring a weather report nobody was watching. Felix had been in the waiting room, doing his homework on fungi for science class, which felt wrong and then, strangely, like the only thing holding him together. His grandfather, a retired biology teacher, had taught him that mushrooms were decomposers, the quiet clean-up crew of the forest. "Nothing wasted," he used to say, tapping the page with two careful fingers.

The funeral was Thursday. Afterward, relatives streamed through Felix's house for what his mother kept calling shiva. He finally asked his cousin Ruth what the word meant. "Shiva is Hebrew for seven," she said, ladling soup. "It's seven days of mourning after the burial, and visitors come to comfort the family." Seven days, Felix thought. A deadline, like the fungi unit test at school.

The problem was that Felix couldn't make himself say anything to anyone. Guests hugged him and told stories, and he nodded like a broken gate. He decided to test an idea: if he couldn't articulate his sadness, maybe he could just be present, standing in the room, listening, the way visitors were apparently supposed to comfort them anyway. So on day five he parked himself beside his great-aunt Miriam, who told a story about Grandpa accidentally setting his own beard on fire at Hanukkah, 1979. Felix laughed so hard that soup nearly came out of his nose, and then, because laughing and crying turned out to run on the same wire, he ended up doing both at once. Great-aunt Miriam patted his knee as if this were perfectly normal, which, in that living room, it was.

His meticulous plan for the eulogy he'd never given, three drafted pages folded in his desk drawer at home, began to feel less necessary. On day six, Mr. Okafor from the hospital, the nurse who had let Felix sneak Grandpa extra pudding, knocked on the door holding a paper bag. "He told me you were studying decomposers," Mr. Okafor said. Inside was a field guide to fungi, with a sticky note in Grandpa's cramped handwriting: For the kid who asks why about everything.

Day seven arrived too fast. Felix sat on the porch steps with Ruth as the last visitors' cars pulled away, the house suddenly quiet in a way that had teeth. Seven days hadn't fixed anything; the deadline just ran out and the sadness kept going. But he opened the field guide to a bracket fungus and read aloud the description of how it slowly turns a dead log into soil for new seedlings, and Ruth leaned her head on his shoulder and said, "He would have made that a whole lesson." "Two lessons," Felix said. "Minimum."

story:
The cemetery gate had a sensor that beeped when someone walked through, and it beeped now for Autumn and her mother and the urn of white flowers they had recruited Aunt Rosa to help arrange. Grandma Pearl's grave was halfway up the hill, the stone still new enough to look like it did not belong yet, standing perpendicular to the slope the way the crew had set it.

Autumn set the urn down and stood with her hands in her pockets. One week ago she had gone to the movies with Priya, four days after the funeral, and she had laughed so hard at some scene about a raccoon in a mailbox that she'd cried. Then she'd stopped, right there in the dark theater, because it felt wrong. Grandma Pearl was in the ground and Autumn was laughing at a raccoon. She hadn't told anyone, not even Priya, who had noticed anyway and asked if she was okay.

"Turn it toward the road," her mother said, tilting the urn so the flowers faced downhill. "That's how she'd want it. Showing off."

"She never showed off," Autumn said.

"She showed off quietly." Her mother knelt and pulled a weed from the base of the stone, then sat back on her heels. "You've been quiet too. Quieter than you think I notice."

Autumn picked at the label on the urn. She could ask now or carry it another week, and she'd already carried it for seven days, and it hadn't gotten lighter. "At the movies I laughed," she said. "Like, a lot. It was three days after the funeral and I laughed until I cried." She stared at the grass. "I keep thinking I did something wrong."

Her mother didn't answer right away. She brushed dirt from her knees and looked at the stone, at PEARL ALVAREZ, 1947 to this year, and Autumn braced herself for a correction.

"Remember when I took that psychology class at the community college, the year you were in fourth grade?" her mother said. "There was a researcher named Margaret Stroebe and another one named Henk Schut. In 1999 they described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life. They called it the dual process model."

"Dual process model," Autumn repeated. Back and forth. Loss, then daily life, then loss again.

"So laughing at a raccoon is part of it?"

"That's the getting-on-with-daily-life part, yes. And being sad here is the other part. You're allowed to do both. You're supposed to do both."

Autumn thought about testing it, the way she'd test an idea in science class. Yesterday she'd made herself look at Grandma's mug on the shelf and had to sit down from the ache of it. Today she'd hummed along with the radio without noticing until the song was over. Back, then forth. Maybe the guilt was just her misreading the data.

A wind came up the hill and bent the white flowers toward the road, showing off for nobody, and Autumn squatted to turn the urn a little more, just to be sure.

"There," she said. "That's better."

story:
The lights went out at 7:40, right in the middle of Nicholas's homework. He sat still and listened. No wind outside, no crash, no siren. The whole street was dark, every window on the block, so the problem was somewhere upstream, a line or a substation he would never see. "It's not fair," Marta said. "Owls can hunt in the dark. Why can't we?"

"We're not nocturnal," Nicholas said. "But wait." He had noticed something while carrying the sandwiches. Twenty minutes ago he had to feel his way along the wall. Now, from the couch, he could see the outline of the armchair, the shape of the bookshelf, the dark rectangle of the doorway to the hall. He hadn't lit another candle. Nothing had changed except time.

He set his phone timer and told Marta to watch the room, not the candle. "Tell me what you can see," he said every few minutes. At first she said nothing, just the couch. Then the lamp. Then the lamp and the window. He remembered a line from a library book about deep-sea divers and dark caves, something about the eyes building back a pigment in the rod cells. "It's called rhodopsin," he said. "It takes half an hour or more to come back. That's the mechanism, I think. Your eyes get more sensitive the longer you sit in the dark."

By the time the timer hit thirty minutes, Marta could count the game pieces on the table without leaning over them. They set up the board, moved their pieces by the gray light, and didn't knock anything over. Somewhere outside, a truck rumbled past, and the street stayed dark, but in the living room Marta moved her piece to the final square and said, "Checkmate."

Piper sat on the low wall at the edge of the skate park, her left arm in a bright green cast, watching her friend Dara drop into the bowl. Two weeks ago that had been her. The doctor pointed to a line that stopped halfway across, like a crack in a sidewalk that runs out of steam.

Now she couldn't stop thinking about it. She'd asked her little brother to bring her a green branch from the backyard, and yesterday, while nobody was watching, she'd pressed her thumb against it. The bark split on one side only, and the branch bowed away on the other, still connected. That was her bone. That was why kids got this kind of break, the doctor had said, because their bones are more flexible than adults'. Older bones snap clean, like dry kindling. Younger ones bend first and crack on just the one side.

"You're doing the branch thing again," Dara said, rolling up beside her with a clatter. She nodded at the twig in Piper's right hand.

"Watch," Piper said. She bent it slowly, splitting the bark a little more. "One side cracks, the other side bends. I keep wondering if my arm would've snapped all the way through if I'd fallen harder. Or if I was, like, eighty."

Dara laughed, then went quiet, spinning her board under one foot. "I always thought a broken bone was a broken bone. Like, all the way or nothing." She frowned at the branch. "So your arm's not really broken?"

"It is," Piper said. "It's just broken on one side and bent on the other." She set the twig down carefully, the way you'd set down evidence. "I'm going to invest my whole recovery in figuring out how it heals. Does the bent side pull the cracked side back straight? Or does the crack fill in first?"

"That's a lot of thinking for a kid with a cast," Dara said, but she was squinting at the branch now too.

Piper traced a line down the middle of the twig with her finger. "This is like the equator of the branch. One half splits, one half holds. If I taped the split side, could the bendy side still flex?" She looked up at the bowl, where sunlight made a bright curve of the concrete. "Next week I get the short cast, the one that lets my elbow move. Doctor says skating again in a month might be feasible if the X-ray looks right."

Dara kicked her board up into her hand. "Race you to the vending machine, then."

Piper was already off the wall, green cast swinging, running on legs that worked just fine.

story:
Eleanor's problem had a name, and the name was Mr. Okafor's worksheet: "Use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s." She sat in the school library with a photocopied page of a settler's diary in front of her, and the diary refused to cooperate. "The land here is flat as a griddle," the settler had written, "and my wife has planted hollyhocks perpendicular to the fence, which she says will fool the wind." That told Eleanor exactly nothing about why anyone had dragged a wagon across half a continent. She flipped the page over. The library's copy machine had accidentally printed part of the next article on the back, something about President Wilson and a peacekeeping body called the League of Nations.

Marcus slid into the chair across from her and stole her pencil. "Still fighting that worksheet? You look like the diary insulted your family."

"It kind of did. This guy writes three paragraphs about hollyhocks." She tapped the back of the page. "But listen to this part. The Senate never ratified the Treaty of Versailles, so the United States never joined the League of Nations. The president helped plan the whole thing, and his own country said no thanks."

Marcus stopped chewing his pencil. "Wait. That's like baking a cake for the whole class and then being the one kid who isn't allowed a slice."

Eleanor laughed, then frowned, then laughed again. "It contradicts everything I assumed. I thought if the president wanted something, it just happened." She copied the sentence onto a sticky note, because it felt like the kind of thing that could sneak up on her later.

Then she went back to the diary with new eyes, hunting for the hidden reason the way she'd hunted for the hidden fact. The settler's grandfather had lost a mill in the East. The land office in Ohio had promised two hundred acres. There it was, buried under the hollyhocks: people moved because of money and land, and the pretty sentences were just decoration. She tested it on the next page. "Sold the clock, kept the rifle, bought seed corn." Money and land again. The pattern held.

"I've got it," she announced. "The diary never says why directly. You have to read past the flowers."

Mr. Okafor wandered by, scanning worksheets like a hawk with a grading pen, and paused at her paragraph. "Evidence?" he asked.

She held up the page. "Lost the mill. Two hundred acres. Sold the clock." Then she added, because she couldn't resist, "Also, the Senate never ratified the Treaty of Versailles, so the United States never joined the League of Nations. Just so you know I know things."

"That's a different unit," said Mr. Okafor, but he was smiling.

"Consider it a preview," said Eleanor, and handed Marcus his pencil back.

story:
The line at Jefferson Elementary School stretched past the bike racks, and Muhammad stood at the very end of it, holding his grandmother's coupon book while she searched her bag for her voter card. A folding table near the double doors held a display he hadn't expected: a large poster titled "Know Your Rights," with articles from the Constitution copied out in careful block letters.

"Read it to me," his grandmother said, squinting at the small print. "My glasses are somewhere in this bag, and we're not losing our place in line."

Muhammad read the First Amendment aloud, then the Fourth, then stopped at one about due process. "It says no state can deprive any person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law," he read slowly. "Baba, what does that mean, really?"

"It means," she said, "you tell me."

He thought while the line shuffled forward. "It means the government can't just take your stuff or lock you up because it feels like it. There has to be a real process. Steps. Like... a foundation under a house. You can't skip it." She nodded but said nothing more, which meant he was on his own.

A man ahead of them was grumbling into his phone. "They passed the water bill, then they didn't pass it. How can both be true in one week? I'm telling you, it's rigged."

Muhammad's ears turned warm. That was the bill his social studies teacher had put on the board Monday. He remembered two different wordings, two headlines, one saying passed and one saying stalled. Something clicked into place, though he couldn't see it yet, like a pattern hiding under a floor.

"Excuse me," Muhammad said to the man. "Was it the House version or the Senate version?"

The man lowered his phone. "House voted Tuesday. Senate voted today on their own copy. Different words in it, the radio said."

"A bill has to pass both the House and the Senate in identical form," Muhammad said, the rule assembling itself out loud, "before it goes to the president. So if the words aren't the same, it's not law yet. Both things you heard can be true."

The man stared at him, then at his phone, then laughed. "Twelve years old and you just untangled the news for me."

The voting machine emitted a low beep as the man stepped up to it, and the line moved again. Muhammad's grandmother had stopped rummaging. She was looking at him with an expression he couldn't read.

"Say the due process one again," she said. "In your own words. My friend Rosa is inside working the table, and she argues with everybody about that one."

"She argues?"

"Every election. You'll see." She took his hand and pulled him toward the doors. "And don't be polite about it."

story:
Michael sat cross-legged on the rug in Dara's basement, laptop balanced on a stack of board games. The plan was simple: a web page called the Prime-o-Matic, with a giant centred heading and a box where you could type a number and find out if it was prime. He had typed the HTML first, then added the CSS, and the heading still sat stubbornly in the top left corner like it had been glued there.

"Did you save the file?" Dara asked from the couch, where she was rolling a tennis ball along the armrest. "The browser can't retrieve the new styles unless you save first."

Michael clicked save, then hit refresh. The heading drifted to the centre of the page, dark blue and enormous, and he sat back with the satisfied feeling of a door finally swinging open on the second try. The page asked a question in plain grey text: Enter a number. He typed 7, pressed the button, and the page said 7 is prime. Correct. He tried 9, and it said 9 is not prime, also correct. Dara came over and typed 97. Prime. They were halfway to a victory snack when she said, "Try zero."

He typed 0 and pressed the button. The page said, in cheerful green letters, 0 is prime.

"That's wrong," Dara said. "Zero isn't prime. It isn't anything." Michael stared at the green line and felt a small, cold drop of despair, the kind you get when something you built confidently turns on you. The checker worked by trying every divisor starting at 2, so for zero the loop found nothing to reject it with, and the code fell through to the prime answer. He couldn't see the loop failing; he could only see its wrong result, like footprints in snow with no animal in sight.

"Okay," he said slowly. "The loop starts at 2. Zero, and 1 too probably, and negative numbers, they never get tested, they just sneak past." He rolled the thought around, then typed an approximate guess at the fix, a single line near the top of the function, and refreshed. Dara typed 0 again. The page said 0 is not prime. Then 1. Not prime. Then -5, and the page held the line: not prime. All the numbers below 2 got sorted out before the loop even began, which was where they belonged.

"So it only checks real candidates now," Dara said, and typed 11, and the heading glowed blue above the words 11 is prime.

"Boom," Michael said, and reached over to change the heading's colour to green.

story:
Blake sat cross-legged on Dara's basement carpet, staring at a laptop screen that stared back with an error message. He had typed nine lines of Python, and the program had refused him nine times.

"It says invalid syntax," he said. "Again."

Dara leaned over from her beanbag, headphones around her neck. "You forgot the colon after the for loop. You always forget the colon."

"I do not always forget the colon." Blake scrolled up, found the missing dot, and added it. The goal was simple: the program would ask for a number, then print whether that number was prime. Dara had bet him a bag of chips he couldn't finish it before dinner. Blake wanted those chips more than he wanted to admit.

He ran the program again. It asked for a number, so he typed 7. "7 is prime," the screen announced. He typed 9. "9 is prime." Blake groaned. "Nine is not prime. Three times three. It's the most not-prime number there is."

"So your checker is broken," Dara said. "It can't see the factors hiding in there."

Blake thought about that. The factors were invisible until you actually divided. That was the whole trick. A number could look prime and secretly be a product of smaller numbers, and the only way to know was to test it. "Okay," he said slowly, "what if I try dividing by every number up to the square root? If any of them divides evenly, it's not prime."

"You're going to replicate the test for each divisor?" Dara asked. "Like, loop it?"

"Exactly like loop it." He rewrote the middle of the program, mumbling to himself, deleted a stray semicolon that had wandered in from somewhere, and ran it again. 9 came back "not prime." So did 15. So did 21, that obstinate little fake. He tried 13, 17, 97. Prime, prime, prime.

"Pay up," Blake said, holding out his hand.

Dara tossed him the chips, then pulled her laptop close and opened Scratch, dragging a sound block into a loop. A record scratch blatted out of her speakers, and she wiggled a sprite back and forth with it.

"You know why it's called Scratch, right?" she said. "DJ scratching. A DJ moves a record back and forth on a turntable to remix sounds."

Blake crunched a chip. "So you're basically a DJ. Except your turntable is code."

"And you're the consumer of my art," Dara said, hitting the green flag again.

The record scratched. Blake typed 2 into his program, and the screen said, "2 is prime."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
story:
The first night at Camp Windrock, Alyssa lay awake listening to a girl named Priya breathe in the bunk above her. By the second night she noticed the pattern: Priya stopped unpacking whenever the lake test came up, chewed her thumbnail raw, and snapped at anyone who touched her duffel bag. On Wednesday, Priya got aggressive over a borrowed hairbrush and then cried behind the boathouse, and Alyssa sat down next to her in the gravel.

"You get stressed before the swim test," Alyssa said. "I can tell because of your hands."

Priya stared at her. "You noticed that?"

"My mom taught me the signs. Mine is stomachaches. Watch." Alyssa counted Priya's breaths out loud, slow ones, four counts in and six counts out, the way the camp mentor had shown the whole cabin after lights-out. Then she said, "You're not sleeping either. I hear you turning over like the top bunk is orbiting the earth all night."

Priya laughed a wet, hiccuppy laugh. After a minute she whispered, "Sometimes I think about hurting myself. Just to make everything stop. Don't tell anyone. Promise?"

Alyssa's promise rose in her throat and then stuck there. She thought hard. Keeping secrets was a rule she'd always followed, but a promise that could let her friend get hurt wasn't a rule at all, it was a trap. She remembered the counselor saying exactly one thing at orientation: if a friend talks about hurting themselves, you tell a trusted adult right away, even if they asked you to keep it a secret. Alyssa had thought it was strange advice at the time. Now it felt like a flashlight in a dark tent.

"I can't promise that," she said, standing up and dusting gravel off her shorts. "Come with me or I'll drag you. Your choice. I'm very strong, I did the ropes course."

"You're the worst secret keeper alive," Priya said, but she got up too.

They found Counselor Dana by the fire pit, and Alyssa said the whole thing in one breath before her courage escaped. Dana didn't lecture anyone or look disappointed. She put her arm around Priya and said, "I'm really glad Alyssa walked you over. That took guts from both of you." Then she told Priya they'd call her parents together in the morning, and that tonight she'd sleep in the quiet room next to the infirmary, with a fan and no top bunk orbiting above her.

That night Alyssa did her own slow breathing, four in and six out, and made a deal with herself: phone in the duffel at nine, headlamp off at nine-thirty, lights out. In the morning Priya appeared at breakfast with her hair actually brushed and slid a tray of hash browns across the table.

"For the worst secret keeper alive," Priya said. "Extra crispy."

"I'll take it," Alyssa said, and stole her orange juice too.

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
story:
Penelope unrolled the climate map across the picnic table and weighted its corners with two flashlights and a bag of trail mix. Tomorrow night, back home, she had to stand up in geography class and explain how a monsoon forms and why rice farmers in South Asia depend on it, and right now she could not make the map cooperate. Tiny letter codes, Af and BWh and Am, were printed in the oceans and across the continents, and she had no idea what they meant. Her little brother, Marcus, leaned over her shoulder with a marshmallow stick still in his hand.

"What do the letters say?" he asked, poking at the Bay of Bengal.

"They say I'm going to fail," Penelope said, and he laughed, which was not helpful.

She pulled out her phone, which had one shaky bar of signal at the edge of the campground, and typed the codes in. The screen loaded slowly, like something dragging itself uphill. The letters, she read, were part of the Koppen climate classification, still used on climate maps today. It had been developed by Wladimir Koppen, a climatologist born in Russia who worked in Germany. She said the name out loud twice so it would stick.

"Koppen," Marcus repeated, chewing his marshmallow stick. "Sounds like a kind of cookie."

The code for the monsoon lands of South Asia was Am, and that was the piece she needed. She thought back to a demonstration her teacher had done in the fall, before the teacher announced she would retire at Christmas. She had set a hairdryer over a pan of sand and a pan of water, and the sand had heated fast while the water had stayed cool, and over the water a little wheel of paper had spun because air was rising there and pulling air in from the sand side. Penelope had understood it then, but standing at a picnic table she needed to test it herself, because tomorrow she would have to make thirty kids see a wind they could not see. She filled one pot from the water jug and left the other empty, set both in the sun on the table, and laid a strip of paper between them, pinned with a pebble so it could swing like a compass needle. Then she waited, drawing the monsoon arrows into her notebook, a symmetrical pair of curves, one pointing toward the land in summer and one reversing in winter, when the land cooled faster than the ocean and the flow turned around. Rice needed the summer flood of rain those onshore winds carried; without it, the paddies cracked dry.

After twenty minutes the paper strip trembled and drifted, gently but definitely, toward the empty pot, the hot dry one. Air over the hot pot was rising and air was creeping in to replace it. It was small, but it was real, and it meant her explanation was true at the scale of a kitchen pot and at the scale of a continent.

"Watch," she said to Marcus, and she cupped her hands and breathed warm air over the wet pot while he shaded the dry one with his jacket. The strip shifted again, wobbling back the other way.

"Did we just make a monsoon?" Marcus asked.

Penelope folded the map, careful with the corners, and grinned at the paper needle still swinging between the pots. "We just made a monsoon."

story:
Jordan had read the text forty times since Friday. "Meet me at the gate at 7," Marisol had written, "my little brother's tagging along, hope that's ok." Then a second message: "don't laugh, he's obsessed with you ever since you taught him that card trick." Jordan had typed and deleted six replies before sending a thumbs up, which now seemed like the lamest response in history.

He stood by the gate with two hot chocolates and one dollar left in his pocket, watching the crowd funnel past the ticket lady whose whole job seemed to be enforcing the no-outside-drinks rule. When Marisol appeared, waving, with a nine-year-old in a puffy coat trailing behind her, Jordan felt as exposed as the away team's kicker, standing alone on the field with everyone watching. His face went hot, and he knew without a mirror exactly how red he looked, because his cheeks felt like they were radiating heat into the cold October air.

"Dominic, you remember Jordan," Marisol said.

"The card trick guy!" Dominic shouted. "Do it again."

Jordan tried the trick. His hands were shaking and he fumbled the double lift, and Marisol laughed, which made him grin, which made his face burn even worse. He turned toward the fence and pretended to study the scoreboard.

"It's blushing," said Dominic, with the authority of a kid who had recently done a report on it. "My science teacher says blushing is when blood vessels in your face widen and more blood flows near the skin."

"Okay, emperor of embarrassing facts," Marisol said, poking her brother, whose coat had a gold collar like the team's penguin mascot, the Emperor.

Jordan half listened, but something snagged in his brain. Widen. More blood near the skin. If widening made red, maybe narrowing made less red. He couldn't see his own vessels, couldn't see blood moving anywhere, but he could test the idea. He pressed the cold hot chocolate cup against each cheek, one, then the other, like a man applying aftershave.

"What are you doing?" Marisol asked.

"Nothing," he said. "Cold cup."

By the third quarter, Dominic had abandoned them for the concession stand and Marisol scooted close on the cold bleacher. "You don't have to hide when you blush, you know," she said quietly. "It's kind of the best thing about you."

Jordan didn't believe her, but he put the cup down anyway, letting his cheeks do whatever they wanted, even when she laughed at his terrible joke about the referee. Then Dominic came sprinting back with a foam finger and a problem: he'd spent their bus money on it. Marisol dug through her pockets and found nothing, and Jordan found one dollar and a lot of silence.

They walked the two miles home in the dark, all three of them, taking turns wearing the foam finger. Marisol held his hand somewhere around the fourth block, and somewhere around the sixth, Dominic snatched the last of the hot chocolate without asking. Jordan let him keep it.
