story:
Jaxson had signed up for the talent showcase because Mr. Ferro left the sign-up sheet on the auditorium door for two weeks, which felt almost like a dare. Now he stood backstage with the school's borrowed guitar, and the sixth string sounded wrong. Not slightly wrong. Totally, embarrassingly wrong, like a bear groaning while everyone else was singing.

The showcase started in twenty minutes. He had learned three chords over a month of lunchtime practice in the empty auditorium, and his whole song depended on that string sounding right. He sat on the edge of the stage, turned the tuning peg, and the note sank even lower. He turned it again, the same direction, and the note dropped again, deep and fuzzy.

He stopped with his hand still on the peg. Okay, he thought. Something was happening here that he could not see. The string was doing something when he turned the peg, and turning it that way made the sound go lower, every single time. So the direction mattered, and whatever invisible thing made the note was being changed by it. He turned the peg the other way, slowly, and the note climbed, rising tighter and brighter until it passed the right pitch and kept going. He backed off a hair. The string settled into a clear, steady tone, and when he pressed his chord, the whole thing rang instead of groaning.

"Is that the trick?" a voice asked. Priya from homeroom was crouched by the curtain rail, holding a violin case that hindered her view of the stage. She had signed up too, and her hands had been shaking since third period, though she kept her face neutral about it.

"It's a pattern," Jaxson said. "The tighter you make the string, the faster it vibrates, so the note goes higher. Loosen it and the vibration slows down and the pitch drops." He plucked the string, tightened it a touch, and plucked again so she could hear the rise. "I loosened it wrong twice before I figured out which way the peg even went."

Priya set down her case and tried it on her violin's E string, turning her peg a sliver, listening, turning back. Her note steadied, and her shoulders came down an inch. She looked at Jaxson like he'd handed her something. "Play it for me?" she said. "The song. I want to hear it while nobody's out there yet."

He glanced at the half-empty rows of seats, then at the little label on the guitar's headstock that read steel and bronze alloy strings. Fine strings, he decided, even if they took figuring out. He set his fingers on the first chord, and Priya settled into the front row, tapping her violin bow softly against her knee to give him a beat.

The bus home from Marsh Creek Elementary had eleven minutes of road between the last stop and Edouard's, and he had decided those eleven minutes would be the new meeting room for the Chess Club. He stood at the front, holding his notebook open against a pole, and read from the page he had titled "Agenda."

"Item one," he said. "The problem of Marcus and Devon."

The two boys glared at each other from opposite seats. Marcus had accused Devon of taking the club's good clock, the one Edouard had saved four weeks of allowance to acquire, and Devon swore he had only borrowed it for his cousin's birthday party and brought it back with a cracked corner. Nobody had seen the crack appear. The club had been fighting about it for so long that Ms. Ruiz called it "chronic" and had threatened to shut the club down if they couldn't settle it themselves.

"I just want us to be friends again," Marcus said, arms crossed. "Can we just do that? Be friends again?"

Devon shrugged. "Fine. Friends."

Edouard wrote "friends again" in his notebook and felt uneasy, though he couldn't say why. It seemed too easy. He kept thinking about it while the bus rattled over the railroad tracks, and finally he flipped back a page. At his grandfather's church, when two neighbors quarreled, they didn't just say sorry. There was a meeting, and at the end each person agreed to specific actions they would each take, so each one knew exactly what he had promised. That was the part Edouard had thought was boring. Now it didn't seem boring at all. It seemed like the missing component, the piece that made "friends again" actually stick.

"Wait," Edouard said. "Marcus, what will you do tomorrow? Say the exact thing."

"Be nice to him, I guess."

"That's not a specific action. Say what, exactly."

Marcus blew out a breath. "Fine. I'll stop calling him Clock Thief at lunch. Out loud, anyway."

Devon looked at the floor. "I'll ask before I take anything from the club box. Every time. And I'll bring my dad's screwdriver Thursday to try to fix the corner."

They both said it again, slower, so Edouard could write it down word for word. He tore the page out, split it in half, and handed each of them the piece with his own promise on it. "Now you each know exactly what you promised," Edouard said. "Item two. Tournament snacks." He tapped his pen against the notebook and waited, but both boys were still reading their half-pages.

Marcus folded his and put it in his shirt pocket, patted it once, and said, "Thursday. Screwdriver. I'll hold you to it."

story:
The porch boards of the meeting house were warm under Camille's bare feet, and beyond the carved doorway the valley lay green and fertile, stitched with sheep and a single winding river. She had the prayer folded in her back pocket, though she wasn't supposed to need it by Sunday. Her coming-of-age ceremony would be held right here on the marae, in front of everyone, and her part was a karakia she had to carry in her head, word by word, the way her grandmother had carried it before her. She kept forgetting the middle stanza. Every time she reached it, the words scattered like birds.

Hemi found her there after school, sweat-dark shirt sticking to his back. He was practicing the haka his kapa haka group would perform for the school welcome on Friday, and he wanted an audience. "Watch my stance," he said, dropping low, fists against his thighs. "I had to modify it. My knee." He launched into the chest-slapping, foot-stamping chant, and though Camille had heard Ka Mate a hundred times at rugby matches, she realized she had never once wondered what the words actually meant. She only knew they made the hair on her arms stand up.

"What are you saying?" she asked when he finished, breathless. "In the words, I mean."

"Ka mate, ka mate, ka ora, ka ora," Hemi said. "It was composed around 1820 by Te Rauparaha, the Ngāti Toa chief. He was hiding from enemies who were chasing him, and when he came out alive, he made the haka to celebrate surviving." He wiped his face with his shirt hem. "It's about being afraid and then not being dead. That's the whole thing."

Camille sat with that. She had always thought the haka was about power, about being terrifying, but underneath the stomping it was about hiding in the dark and coming out. She remembered, suddenly, being nine and refusing to speak at her grandfather's funeral because she was scared of crying in front of everyone, and how her mother had carried her sorry little note to the front instead. She had never decided whether that had been wisdom or cowardice, and she still couldn't. But Te Rauparaha had been chased and had hidden, and the hiding had not been the end of his story. That felt like something, though she couldn't have said exactly what.

She pulled the prayer from her pocket, looked at the middle stanza once, then folded it away and stood up. "Do it again," she said, "and this time I'll do the words with you." When Hemi shouted the first line, Camille's voice cracked on it, then steadied, and the sound they made together rolled out over the porch and down toward the river, which caught the late light and held it like a blade. Behind them, high on the ceiling of the porch, the old electric fan spun its slow propeller circles, pushing the warm air around and around.

On Sunday she would stand in that doorway with nothing in her pockets at all.

The gym had flooded on Tuesday, so Coach Ruiz held the basketball tryouts in Alex's backyard, which meant Alex couldn't be late even if he tried. He stood at the fence in his sneakers, watching nine other kids dribble around the folding chairs Coach Ruiz had set up as cones.

"You're lucky," said Marcus, jogging over. Marcus lived two streets down and had walked over eating a bagel, which he was still finishing. "Tryout at your own house. Home-court advantage."

"You can't have home-court advantage on grass," Alex said.

Marcus shrugged and sat on the porch steps to watch the others, saving his legs, as he put it. He wanted to see who his competition was before wasting any energy. Alex had done something like that once, at last year's tryout, sitting out the warm-up to study the other kids, and then running his sprints like his shoes were full of wet sand. So the night before, he'd run an experiment. His sister Priya had timed him on her phone while he sprinted the length of the backyard cold, and he'd done it in a time neither of them wrote down because it was too depressing. Then he'd tried a gradual warm-up, easy jogging and moving stretches, the kind where you walk and reach and swing your legs rather than hold a stretch still, until he could feel his heart working faster and his legs warmed through. After that, the same sprint was nearly a full second faster. Same boy, same grass, same shoes. The only thing that had changed was the warm-up. Priya had made him do it twice more to be sure, which he suspected was mostly because she enjoyed bossing him around, but the numbers held.

"Line up," Coach Ruiz called. "Shuttle runs first, then layups."

Marcus stayed on the porch steps, observing. Alex started the light jog around the chairs, then the moving stretches, keeping it easy, nothing dramatic. He could feel it happen again: his heart rate climbing, his legs going warm.

"You're going to be tired before we even start," Marcus said from the steps.

"I'm warming up," Alex said. "Light jogging, moving stretches. Gets the heart rate up and the muscles warm."

"That sounds like extra work."

It did sound like extra work, which was maybe the point. When the whistle blew, Alex ran the shuttle like the grass owed him something. His legs answered on the first step instead of the fifth. Marcus, meanwhile, went from sitting to sprinting with nothing in between, and by the third shuttle he was moving like a different, slower boy, one whose shoes were, presumably, full of wet sand. He kept glancing at his own legs with an expression approaching despair.

At the layup station, Marcus missed his first four, all of them short, clanging off the front of the rim. On the fifth he banked it in and raised both arms as if he'd solved something.

"Tired already?" Coach Ruiz asked him.

"Unlucky rims," said Marcus. "Homemade."

Coach Ruiz looked at the portable hoop, then at Marcus, and wrote something on his clipboard that was probably not "unlucky rims."

At the end, Coach Ruiz read the list of names for the travel team. Alex made it, third from the top. Marcus did not make it, and stood by the porch steps staring at the grass like it might apologize.

"I had a bad day," Marcus said.

Alex picked up the folding chairs and started stacking them. "Come over tomorrow. We'll warm up first."

"Warm up," Marcus said, as if the word tasted like the bagel had probably tasted. "Fine. But only because your rims are weird."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
story:
Avery knelt in the dirt beside the tomato plants and counted the wilted leaves again, even though she already knew the answer was seven. Something was stealing water from the bed near the fence, and the thief was invisible. The soaker hose ran the whole length of the garden, but the far end had gone dry, and only the tomatoes on the north side drooped. "It's a reasonable guess," she said to the dog, who panted at her hopefully. "If I say the hose is blocked somewhere in the middle, and I cut the water on and feel along the line, the guess either works or it doesn't."

Her little brother, Marcus, wandered out with a popsicle, which began to irritate her immediately, because he had a way of leaning over her shoulder and dripping. "Miss Kaylee at the science centre says the hose thing is called a hypothesis," he said, as if this settled something.

"You didn't even go to the science centre."

"I did. On the field trip. The guide asked if evolution was real and Thomas said it's 'just a theory,' and the guide said no, a theory is not a guess, it's an explanation that's been tested over and over, and it's been supported every time. A hypothesis is the idea still being tested. Thomas got so red." Marcus licked his popsicle with enormous satisfaction.

Avery turned that over while she ran her fingers along the hose, one knuckle of rubber at a time. Her blocked-hose idea was still just a hypothesis until the test came back. If she found a kink, the test would support it. If the hose ran clear all the way to the end, the idea would be overturned, and she would need a different explanation entirely, maybe a root crushing the pipe under the fence. She kept pressing forward, wetter and wetter, and just past the basil she felt a hard, folded lump where the hose had doubled back under a stone.

She moved the stone and straightened the kink, and by the time the popsicle stick was dry, water had reached the far end and darkened the whole strip of soil. The climax came at sunset, when the seven wilted tomatoes lifted their leaves like hands unclenching. "So my guess was supported," Avery said. "I tested it once. I'd have to test it a lot more before it turned into anything like a theory."

"Like a tomato theory," Marcus said.

"Sure," she said, and wrote "hose hypothesis, day one" on a plant tag with a stub of pencil, then pressed it into the mud beside the fence.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
story:
Eli had forty dollars and one goal: a Slither Snake keychain, the holographic kind that had sold out at three stores already. He'd commuted to the mall on the early bus just to beat the Saturday crowd, and the fourth store, a cramped shop near the food court, still had a sign in the window that read HOLOGRAPHIC SNAKES HERE.

The shopkeeper lifted the last one off the hook behind the counter. "Thirty-five dollars," she said, watching him count.

"That's double what they cost last month," Eli said.

"They're scarce now. Everybody wants one." She set it on the glass, and a girl behind him in line sighed loudly.

Eli paid, mostly to stop the sighing girl from grabbing it, and walked out holding the little bag like it might dissolve. In the atrium he passed his friend Marcus, who was sitting on a bench with a shoebox full of homemade woven bracelets. A hand-lettered card leaned against it: BRACELETS $8.

"Eight?" Eli said. "Maya sells hers for five."

"Maya sold out twice," Marcus said. "Hers are the cool ones now. I figured if hers go for eight at the fair, mine could too." He had sold exactly nothing so far, and his shoulders said so.

Eli sat down beside him and turned the keychain over in his fingers, thinking about the line behind him at the shop, the empty hooks, the sign in the window. Something was connecting itself in his head, a pattern he couldn't quite see yet, like a rule working behind the glass where nobody watched. High price, sold out, everybody wanting one. He looked at Marcus's bracelet box again, then at the wide mall hallway stretching toward the food court.

"Stay here," Eli said. "Watch my snake."

He walked the length of the hallway and back, slow and observant, like a detective in one of the memoirs his grandmother kept lending him. In front of the fountain, two more kids had set out boxes of woven bracelets, nearly identical to Maya's style, each marked $8. Near the escalator, a third. An older girl with an agile, quick-fingered weaving style was working a loom right on the floor, threads flying, a finished stack beside her. Eli counted the bracelet sellers he could see from one spot. Seven.

He came back and put the box lid on Marcus's bracelets. "Follow me," he said, and carried the box to the fountain, where he set it down beside the older girl's stack. "How many have you sold?" he asked her.

She squinted at him. "You're the fourth person to set up in the last hour. I've sold two since noon." Around the fountain, buyers strolled past boxes that now outnumbered them, and Eli watched one kid walk the whole circle, comparing, and buy nothing.

Then Maya herself appeared, coming down the escalator with an empty tray and a look of disbelief. "I sold out at eight dollars," she said, "so I raised to ten. But look at this." She waved a hand at the crowded circle of sellers. "Where did all these come from?"

"Sellers usually offer more when the price rises," Eli said. "Making and selling them gets more profitable, I guess. So everybody jumped in."

Maya bit her lip. "Then ten dollars is wrong now."

"Five is wrong the other way," Marcus said slowly. "When there's this many, cheap wins."

Maya flipped her sign to four dollars, and within minutes a small knot of kids had gathered at her table, because hers were the originals and everyone knew it. Eli leaned against the fountain's cool stone, holding his snake keychain in plain view.

A boy elbowed his friend and pointed. "Whoa, a holographic one. What'd that cost you?"

Eli looked at the bag, then at the crowded fountain behind him, and said, "Thirty-five. But if I were you, I'd wait two weeks."

"Two weeks for what?"

Eli held up the snake so it caught the light and shimmered. "For everybody who saw me buy this to start making them."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
story:
Samantha stood at the counter of Horizon Travel with two brochures spread in front of her and a graph printout pinned under her elbow. The agent, Ms. Delgado, had given her rainfall and temperature charts for the Sonoran Desert and the Amazon rainforest as homework, and tomorrow her class would debate which place their imaginary trip should go. Samantha wanted to win that debate, and she wanted to win it with numbers, not opinions.

"Look at this," she said, tapping the rainfall bars for the desert. "Almost nothing for ten months, then a short spike. The rainforest gets heavy rain every single month." Ms. Delgado leaned over the counter. "And temperature?"

"Desert swings wild. Boiling days, cold nights. Rainforest stays warm all year, barely changes." Samantha laid the two temperature lines side by side. "So the desert's line looks like a roller coaster and the rainforest's looks flat."

"That wasn't random," Ms. Delgado said, smiling. "I picked those two on purpose. They demonstrate the extremes better than any other pair."

Behind them, Samantha's father was hunched over a topographic map of a road near the rainforest lodge, part of the same trip package. He was a cyclist and he'd been quiet for five minutes, which meant trouble. "Sam, come look. There's a climb between the lodge and the river. The contour lines say we rise about 100 meters, and the map scale shows that happens over 500 meters of road. Is that rideable?"

Samantha pulled out her notebook. "You divide the rise in height by the horizontal distance." She wrote 100 over 500. "That's one fifth." She multiplied by 100. "It's a 20 percent grade."

Her father lowered the map. "Twenty percent. That's brutal. I'd be walking most of it."

"So don't take that road," Samantha said. She traced an alternate route on the map, a longer one that curved around the ridge. Her dad checked the contours, checked the scale, and let out a breath.

At home that evening, Samantha built her whole debate argument on the same foundation: the graphs showed the desert as extreme and the rainforest as steady, and steady meant predictable, and predictable meant a better trip. She practiced twice in front of the mirror, then marked her favorite line with a yellow highlighter.

At school the next morning, Marcus, her debate opponent, slapped his own desert poster on the board. "Desert wins," he announced, "because adventure."

Samantha held up her charts. "Numbers first."

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
story:
Lucas had half an hour before his grandmother's restaurant opened, and three things had to reach the table together: rice, curry, and flatbread. She refused to help with the timing. "A cook who cannot finish a meal at once," she said, tapping the big clock above the stove, "serves cold rice." So he stood in the hot kitchen with his notebook, writing numbers. Rice took twenty minutes. Curry took forty. Flatbread cooked in two minutes a piece, but the dough had to rest for fifteen. He worked backward from six o'clock, starting the curry first, then the rice, then the dough, and saving the flatbreads for last.

The curry needed onions, and that was where everything stopped. The cutting board sat on the end of a table with one short leg, so the whole surface tilted whenever he pressed down. He set an onion on it and reached for the knife, and the onion rolled straight off the board and bounced onto the floor. He picked it up, set it down more gently, and turned to grab a bowl. When he looked back, it had rolled again, off the edge and into the bin of potato peelings. The wobbly table wanted everything to slide toward the low corner, and the round onion had no way to stay put.

He thought about his grandfather then, and the camping trip two summers ago. They had chopped vegetables on a folding table by the lake, and Lucas remembered watching him cut an onion in half from top to root before slicing it, then laying each half flat side down. The halves had sat perfectly still on that uneven table while his grandfather's knife worked fast and even. At the time Lucas had thought it was just how old people did things, slow and systematic, one extra step that a kid would skip. His grandfather had even said, "You have to halve it first, top to root, or it runs away from you." Lucas had laughed and gone to look for frogs.

Now he washed the onion, cut it in half from top to root, and laid each half flat side down on the board. Neither one moved. He sliced carefully, and even when the table wobbled under his pressure, the halves stayed where he put them. He finished the onions in half the time the rolling ones had cost him, dropped them into the pot, and got the curry going at ten past five, right on schedule.

While the curry simmered, he started the rice and mixed the flatbread dough, setting it under a cloth to rest. He wiped down the board and thought about his grandfather again. Maybe he should have paid more attention that summer, instead of assuming every lesson was boring until it was needed. Or maybe that was just how learning went, and nobody could hurry it. He glanced at the clock, pressed a flatbread into the hot pan, and watched it bubble.

At six exactly, his grandmother came through the swinging door. She looked at the steaming pot, the fluffy rice, the stack of warm flatbreads, all of them ready together. She tore a piece of bread, scooped up curry, and ate it standing. Then she pointed her spoon at the cutting board, where one onion half still sat flat and unmoving, waiting for the next order. "So," she said, "the frogs were not worth it after all?"

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and cold coffee, and posters of smiling candidates saturated the walls around the folding tables where people lined up to vote. Aria stood beside her grandfather, holding the homework sheet her teacher had assigned: read one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and explain it in your own words. She had picked the sheet of paper out of a pile an hour ago because it looked short. Now she wished she had picked a longer one, because the short one made no sense.

"Section 3," she read under her breath. "Every citizen of Canada has the right to vote in an election of members of the House of Commons or of a legislative assembly."

"You're muttering," her grandfather said. He was next in line.

"I have to explain it. In my own words. To the whole class." She looked up at the sign above the registration table. It said who could vote: Canadian citizens, eighteen or older, living in the riding. Aria stared at it. The sign didn't mention the Charter at all. So where did the right actually come from? Was it from the sign, or from something behind the sign?

She tested her idea the only way she could think of. She walked to the woman at the registration table, a gray-haired lady with a lanyard, and asked, "If the sign says who can vote, does the sign decide?"

The woman shook her head. "The sign is just a reminder. Section 3 of the Charter gives every Canadian citizen the right to vote in elections for the House of Commons and the provincial legislatures. That's what decides."

Aria wrote fast, then stopped. "Wait. Provincial too? Not just federal?"

"Provincial legislatures too," the woman said, and pointed at a voter heading toward a booth. "You could ask him. He's here for the provincial one, not the federal."

The man grinned. "There's more than one kind of election, kid. Same right covers both."

Back in line, Aria tried the words out loud, quietly, then rewrote them twice. When her grandfather came out of the booth, she read it to him in the parking lot, her breath fogging in the October air. "So the Charter, Section 3, means if you're a citizen, voting is a right you have, not a favor someone hands you, and it counts for the big federal election and for your province's legislature too. Conventional rules, like the sign, just tell you the details of how."

Her grandfather zipped his coat. "Say that Monday. Word for word."

She folded the paper into her pocket, right beside the stub he let her keep, the one with the little pencil smudge on it.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
story:
The message sat on Mia's screen like a dropped plate: "Great, so everyone's ditching the science project. Might as well fail together." That wasn't what she meant at all. She had typed "Let's just give up on the volcano idea, we're doomed" as a joke, and Priya had taken it literally, and now Devon was typing "wait what" and the ten-slide presentation was due at eight tomorrow morning.

Mia tried to fix it with "kidding!!" but the damage had a way of lingering. Priya replied with a single period, which somehow felt worse than yelling. Devon sent "I stayed up till eleven on the lava diagram," and Mia could picture him at his desk, shoulders sinking. She remembered, suddenly, a time last spring when she'd been on the other side of it. A boy in her English class had posted "your essay was hilarious" under her story about her grandmother, and she'd spent a whole weekend believing he was mocking her before a friend explained it was a compliment. She remembered the flat, stuck feeling of it, a kind of emotional plateau she couldn't climb off until someone cleared things up.

There had to be a better way, so she did what she always did with unsolvable feelings: she turned it into a question. How do people signal jokes in writing? She opened a search window, half-watching the group chat in case Devon started a fight with himself. She typed "how to show a message is a joke" and scrolled past pages of advice until a result caught her eye, something about the very first smiley face.

She read it twice. On September 19, 1982, a computer scientist named Scott Fahlman had proposed the emoticon :-) on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes. Mia sat back. People had been confusing each other in writing for so long that a scientist had invented a symbol to solve it, and that symbol was older than her parents. The sideways face looked ancient now, but its whole job was the exact problem she'd just caused.

She started typing, then stopped. A public apology in the chat might embarrass Priya, who already felt foolish for believing the joke. Instead she sent Priya a private message: "I'm so sorry, that was a joke, badly done. Guess what I just learned?" She pasted the fact, and Priya replied with ":-)" and then "ha, so it's been a problem since 1982," and Mia felt the group chat's coldness begin to thaw, slow and resilient the way friendships usually are.

Back in the main chat, where Devon was still worrying about his lava diagram, Mia posted a picture of her sketchbook, already open to three pages of volcano notes. "Not giving up," she wrote. "I was kidding before. From now on my jokes come with this: :-) Consider it a public service." Devon answered within seconds. "Then put it on the title slide."
